article.title: Gig Economy Is Broken
article.author: Steven Hill
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Okay, so now the Democrats have impressively won sizable majorities in both the Senate and the House. This moment feels somewhat like the fishbowl ending of the movie “The Candidate,” when the victorious stunned Senator-elect, played by Robert Redford, who has just pulled off a major upset, disorientedly asks his campaign manager, “What do we do now?” Indeed: what will the Democrats do now with their majority? Can they solve real problems for everyday Americans? Governing is a lot harder than defeating a badly wounded rabid candidate like Donald Trump. Here’s an idea that would allow Democrats to solve a real problem that has been hurting many American workers as they grapple with changes in the economy. In recent years, the US labor force has been undergoing a fundamental transformation. In today’s “Uber economy,” self-employed workers, contractors, freelancers, gig workers, temps, permatemps, remote workers after COVID and so-called “independent workers” have been championed by Silicon Valley and Wall Street as the “new way to work”—the wave of the future, especially with AI changing the nature of work itself. Many US consumers have driven in an Uber taxi, but don’t realize that most drivers earn below minimum wage after accounting for vehicle expenses, gas, maintenance, and unpaid time waiting for passengers. Those drivers are so-called “independent contractors,” so the billion-dollar Uber is not responsible for providing healthcare, Social Security contributions, injured worker or unemployment compensation, not to mention sick leave or vacation pay. Related: Women Politicians Under Attack: The Growing Threat to Democracy Another type of “gig-preneur” can be found on platforms like Fiverr, an online job brokerage that connects buyers to sellers of numerous tasks and services called micro-gigs. Each gig pays as little as $5 per job (hence, its Fiverr name). One worker, after fulfilling a total of 27 orders, found that she had made a grand total of $176. “I’ve seen panhandlers get more money outside of the 7-11 ,” she complained. Other types of workers swept up in this job market degradation don’t work at gigs, they have regular jobs. Meet Chris Young, an assembly-line worker at a Nissan manufacturing plant in Tennessee. Young works alongside dozens of other employees doing the exact same job, but he doesn’t work directly for Nissan. Instead, he works as a “perma-temp” for Yates Services, a private contractor who provides a majority of Nissan’s workers. He builds the same Infiniti SUV as the Nissan workers, but he and other Yates employees receive half the salary, less job security, and way fewer safety net benefits. Some “temps” have worked at the same company for as long as 11 years—hence the new term “perma-temp.” How many “new economy” workers are there? America is a wealthy nation, but unfortunately these drastic changes to the job markets have resulted in millions of Americans not enjoying the bounty of that wealth. How many of these new economy workers are there? It’s hard to say because they are difficult to count. The Bureau of Labor Statistics counts about 12 million “independent contractors” (7.4% of 162 million workers in the US) and another 2.8 million (1.7%) on-call workers, over 9 percent of the total workforce. But the BLS uses a narrow “worker” definition, and broader definitions push total estimates much higher, from 16.5 million to over 30 million workers, depending on whether researchers count occasional side gigs or secondary jobs. Industry trackers like MBO Partners estimate that r oughly 75 million Americans (46%) engage in some form of independent work yearly, with 22% treating it as their primary full-time career, more than double the 10% who did so in 2019. Related: Why Are Democrats Shooting Themselves in the Foot on Ranked Choice Voting? New app- and Web-based technologies are making it easier than ever to hire such workers. And there is great incentive for employers to do so, especially in certain industries and occupations, to take advantage of what is known as the “independent contractor loophole.” An employer can lower labor costs dramatically by around 30%, just by evading contributions for a worker’s health benefits, Social Security, Medicare, unemployment, injured workers compensation, lunch breaks, paid sick days and vacation leave. Also, a McKinsey report found that independent contractors get paid 20-30% less than employees. So these savings provides a powerful incentive for an employer to hire as many contractors as possible. To be sure, some businesses legitimately benefit from a degree of labor flexibility, since they need to have an ability to ramp up and down in response to fluctuations in demand for their product or service. But hiring a large contractor workforce allows a company to greatly lower its labor costs by wiping out its workers’ safety net, which undermines a key component that has built the middle class and made the US economy so successful. Portable safety net provides the best of both worlds Fortunately, there is an innovative solution to this tension, and the Democrats should jump on this. It’s called a “portable safety net,” or “portable benefits.” It would allow any worker hired by multiple employers during the year to benefit from a robust safety net. Here’s how it works. Each business who hires an independent worker would contribute a certain amount for that worker, above the wage , that is pro-rated according to the number of hours the worker has worked for that employer. Those payroll deductions would be set aside in an Individual Security Account for each worker, with the funds helping that worker to pay for her/his safety net. The ISA accounts would be structured to direct the payroll deductions into existing federal and state safety net programs—Social Security, Medicare, unemployment insurance and injured workers’ compensation—as well for other safety net components, especially health care, and possibly paid sick days and vacation (the worker also would have some wages deducted, much like regularly-employed full-time workers do). Related: From “11,780 Votes” to Trump’s 2026 Election Power Grab For example, suppose Donna is a regular employee working 20 hours a week for a hairdresser, then contracts for 10 hours a week with TaskRabbit, and drives 10 shifts for Uber. She would earn 50 percent of her benefits from the hairdresser, 25 percent from TaskRabbit, and another percentage based on her wages driving for Uber. The funds from each company would be deposited into her ISA. Note that this is similar to the way Social Security and Obamacare work now, in which a retirement account or a health care account is tracked with a personal ID number for individuals who work for multiple employers. A portable safety net for all workers who need it would result in a number of beneficial effects. It would allow some scheduling flexibility for workers and businesses, as well as the health and financial security that workers and their families need. It also would shore up affordability for many individuals and families, especially after the Trump administration’s deep cuts to Medicaid, Medicare, SNAP and other programs. A portable safety net also would move us beyond all the labor abuses and lawsuits over who’s a contractor or regular employee and entitled to safety net coverage, because all workers would be covered . It would remove the perverse incentive for businesses to use cheaper contractors as a way of lowering their labor costs and undercutting their competitors, which unleashes a race to the bottom. Note that requiring all businesses in an industry to pay into their workers’ ISAs would not hurt the competitiveness of any those businesses, because all employers would be subject to the same rules. The costs for this kind of “safety net insurance plan” could be passed on by businesses to their customers, since that is the largest pool capable of absorbing these costs. Many of the customers would also be the same workers receiving benefits, so it would be a virtuous circle, “a rising tide floating all boats.” A number of countries already do something like this. I first proposed it for American workers back in 2015-16 in my book Raw Deal about the “Uber economy,” and in a policy paper for New America , and the idea sort of caught on in public policy circles . It was endorsed by 40 business, government, labor, and NGO leaders from the right and left who agree: it is a necessary foundation for the 21 st century economy. President Barack Obama endorsed portable benefits in his 2016 State of the Union address, and legislation was proposed in state legislatures in New York, Washington and New Jersey. The idea had some legislative momentum but Trump and COVID killed it. Ironically, the only employers at the time who tried the idea was Uber and Lyft for their California operations, but the Individual Security Accounts they offered were so measly as to be nearly worthless. Rather than paying into the ISA something close to the 20% of a worker’s wage that is necessary to provide an adequate safety net, Uber and Lyft offered only 2.5%. And they required minimum “hours worked” thresholds to qualify that most drivers couldn’t reach. Not surprisingly, Uber/Lyft cynically offered the portable benefits as part of their oppositional campaign, Proposition 22, to overturn a California law, AB 5, that required the companies to treat their drivers like regular employees instead of independent contractors. Related: AI Warfare Goes Unchecked So “portable safety net” was a bit ahead of its time, but none of the salient issues have gone away; in fact the need has only increased as the labor force prepares for the tsunami of AI. In the current moment, this would be a great issue for the Democrats to champion. Already there is momentum building in various states . A portable safety net for all workers is an idea whose time has come. It would help ensure that the labor force and the broader economy are placed on a fair and healthy foundation for the future. All Americans deserve to be enriched by technology and innovation, instead of made obsolete or impoverished by it. For the Democrats, this has the makings of a win-win solution. But are Democratic leaders bold enough to seize the opportunity? DemocracySOS
